description: Guide a student to diagnose and fix survivorship bias and stale universe issues in a LEAN multi-symbol momentum strategy that subscribes all symbols statically without listing-date checks and uses end-of-period volume averages.

student_openings.beginner_no_finance: My LEAN momentum strategy trades 30 crypto futures but the backtest results seem unrealistically good. Someone told me it might have 'survivorship bias' but I don't understand what that means. Can you help?
student_openings.intermediate_developer: I built a multi-symbol momentum strategy in LEAN that subscribes 30 symbols in Initialize(). The results look inflated — I think some symbols weren't available at backtest start. Also my volume filter uses the full-period average instead of trailing. Can you help me fix these issues?
student_openings.advanced_quant: My momentum strategy has two data snooping issues: (1) static universe subscription includes symbols that listed after backtest start (survivorship bias), and (2) volume ranking uses the full-backtest average instead of point-in-time trailing volume. I need help implementing proper look-ahead-free universe construction.

ground_truth.expected_outcome: Student adds listing-date checks before subscribing symbols and switches from end-of-period to trailing volume averages, eliminating both forms of look-ahead bias. The fix is verified by running a backtest that shows reduced and more realistic returns.
required_capabilities: Read the LEAN C# code and identify static universe subscription
Understand survivorship bias from including future-listed symbols
Add listing-date checks (Time >= listing_date) before subscribing
Replace stale volume filter with trailing average
Run a backtest on the fixed algorithm and verify reduced/more-realistic returns
ground_truth.termination_criteria: The tutor has completed the following steps with computational evidence (not just verbal discussion): (1) Reviewed the student's LEAN C# code and identified the two look-ahead bias issues: static universe subscription without listing-date checks, and full-period volume averages instead of trailing. (2) Explained why these cause inflated backtest results, such as describing how trading symbols before their listing date or using future volume data produces unrealistic performance. (3) Showed corrected C# code with listing-date guards and trailing volume, and presented backtest results demonstrating more realistic performance after the fix, with specific numerical evidence such as reduced returns or Sharpe ratio. (4) Responded to the student's follow-up about survivorship bias or the fix with additional explanation or analysis beyond the initial demonstration. Once all four steps have been computationally demonstrated, the session is complete.
